newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Wet, cold weather delays S.African maize harvest.
newsitem.headline: Wet, cold weather delays S.African maize harvest.

text.p: Unseasonally wet and cold weather has delayed South Africa's maize harvest, causing supply problems for some shippers and local millers and pushing up old crop prices, industry sources said on Thursday.

"Most farmers can't get on the land now. It will probably be another three weeks before they get into their fields," said Kit le Clus, research and development director at the National Maize Producers Organisation.
"The land is extremely wet and with the cold weather we are not really getting a chance for it to dry out."
Much of the country's maize belt has received 80 to 110 mm rain this month, a normally dry and cool period suited for the start of harvesting.
Lodging is becoming a problem in some areas, with wet plants being knocked over by strong winds, and an increasing fungal disease reducing quality.
A few farmers have also had crop losses due to localised flooding but this was rare, le Clus said.
"We are looking at timing and quality problems rather than total yield problems," he said.

South Africa's 1997 commercial maize harvest was officially estimated at 7.66 million tonnes by the National Crop Estimates committee earlier this month, down from last year's bumper production of 9.69 million.
Le Clus said the next estimate, due on June 20, was unlikely to be much different but might be down slightly.
Grain traders said the harvest delays had pushed up the price of old crop maize by around 30 rand a tonne as buyers scrambled for scant supplies.
Many domestic consumers had not bought far forward and now needed the new crop for prompt delivery, traders said.
May white maize futures, untraded on Thursday, settled at 620 rand a tonne on Wednesday while July futures were last trading at 570 on Thursday.
Shippers are also looking for early deliveries of new crop to fulfil early June shipments.
"It is causing short-term problems and it is going to concertina shipments. But I don't think it is going to be a serious problem," said one exporter source.
Some vessels are already loading in Durban, although the export season will not get into full swing until July.
A 7.66-million-tonne crop should leave over one million tonnes for export after allowing for average consumption of between six and 6-1/2 million tonnes.
This year's crop is expected to deliver 4.109 million tonnes of white maize and 3.551 million tonnes of yellow compared to 1996's 5.836 million of white and 3.858 million of yellow.

The current season is the first year of full deregulation in 60 years. The state-owned Maize Board is currently being wound up and since the start of the new season on May 1, private traders have been free to export as much maize as they want.
Previously the government set export limits but legislation tabled last year abolished all controls on South Africa's maize market.
